note: the pen is still down there — a hand could find it chapters later
anchor: When she knocked on the roof, he jumped so hard the pen went down between the seats.
para: He was in the driver's seat of the taxi in the yard, with both front doors open for the breeze, his chin on his chest and his mouth open, snoring over the little book where he wrote his fares. When she knocked on the roof, he jumped so hard the pen went down between the seats.

options.label: Let it stay lost
options.text: He felt for it with two fingers and gave up.

options.label: Kit sees it, leaves it
options.text: She could see it down there in the gap, the cap of it, and she didn't fish it out, because it was his car and his pen and he'd have said so.

options.label: He asks for it later
options.text: "Leave it," he said, when she bent to look. "I know where it is."

why: Smallest touch. The pen is already planted; the chapter has enough going on. A later hand finds it in the gap.

note: let one of the others not notice at all — Tock walks past the step without a glance, mid-laugh
anchor: Juno always noticed.
para: Juno noticed. Juno always noticed.

options.label: Tock walks past mid-laugh
options.text: Tock went past the step still laughing and didn't turn his head.

options.label: Sol looks through her
options.text: Sol looked straight at the step and didn't see it, the way you don't see a gate you've walked past every day of your life.

options.label: Lyra waves at the wrong house
options.text: Lyra waved, big, with her whole arm, at the upstairs. Nobody lived in the upstairs.

why: Tock is the one who comes to everything angry or laughing; him not registering her at all sets up the look he gives her at the bend in ch 8.

note: what slippers do on a hot hill at a run — slap, heel sliding out, the road through the sole
anchor: Up the hill in her slippers on the hot road, past the hibiscus, to Juno.
para: Up the hill in her slippers on the hot road, past the hibiscus, to Juno.

options.label: Slippers slap and slide
options.text: Up the hill in her slippers, the rubber slapping, her heel sliding off the back every third step so she ran half on the slipper and half on the road, past the hibiscus, to Juno.

options.label: Kick them off
options.text: Up the hill in her slippers until the left one went, and then barefoot on the hot road, past the hibiscus, to Juno.

options.label: Heat through the sole
options.text: Up the hill in her slippers, the road hot through the thin place in the left sole, past the hibiscus, to Juno.

why: Anyone who's run in slippers knows the heel going. Option 2 is good but leaves a slipper in the road the next scene has to account for.

note: a baby that's been wet for hours, held against a shirt — the smell reaches Juno across the kitchen before Tock does
anchor: She was screaming, a thin furious sound, red-faced and soaked through her sleepsuit.
para: He came through the door with the baby against his chest. She was screaming, a thin furious sound, red-faced and soaked through her sleepsuit. Tock kept saying "it's okay, it's okay" in a voice that wasn't. Juno had never in her life been so glad to hear anything scream.

options.label: Smell crosses the kitchen
options.text: The smell of her reached the counter before Tock did, hours of it, hot and sour through the cotton.

options.label: Wet soaks into his shirt
options.text: The front of Tock's shirt was dark where she'd been against it, and he hadn't noticed, or didn't care.

options.label: Her skin, when Juno takes her
options.text: When Juno put a hand on her back the sleepsuit was cold and wet and stuck to the skin underneath, and the skin under that was hot.

why: Smell is the one the reader can't look away from, and it gets to Juno before she can be the one in charge of it.

note: Lonny's the one who'd crack something here, right after the baby — a line that's wrong for the room and lets everyone breathe
anchor: "And then?" Lonny said.
para: "And then?" Lonny said.

options.label: Lonny and the thermos
options.text: "Because I'm not carrying no ninety-year-old man down this road in the dark. Mr. Hale can walk." Nobody laughed. Sol did, once, into her hand, and then they all were, badly, and the baby screamed through it.

options.label: Lonny on the baby
options.text: "She louder than Bix," Lonny said, and Tock made a sound that wasn't a laugh and then was.

options.label: Lonny, about Tock
options.text: "Tock, you walk past a baby," Lonny said. "A whole baby." Tock looked at him. Then Sol laughed, wet, and Tock said "shut up," and it was the first thing anybody had said all night in a normal voice.

why: Option 3 is the group being the group: the target is Tock, the joke is cruel and lets him off at the same time, and 'a whole baby' is the kind of line they'd keep. Note: the anchor the flags file caught is just 'Lonny said.' — the full line is '"And then?" Lonny said.' Insert after that.

note: Juno is lying to herself here — the one place in the chapter her dialect could slip a notch heavier, per the rule that a Trace kid dropping into dialect means something is wrong with them
anchor: We're just the ones up here."
para: "Town has to do town." She said it flat. "There's a hundred kids like us down there right now doing exactly this. Walking into houses. We're not special. We're just the ones up here."

options.label: One notch heavier
options.text: We not special. We just the ones up here."

options.label: Heavier, and she hears it
options.text: We not special. We just the ones up here." She heard herself say it and didn't fix it.

options.label: Only the last word
options.text: We're not special. We just up here."

why: The rule says don't remark on it. Option 1 lets it slip and moves on; the reader who's listening will hear it. Option 2 is the narrator noticing, which rule 14 forbids.

note: this inventory wants to be obsessive — Juno would read the labels, the expiry dates, the one box that's half-used; she's the table-learner
anchor: Inside: a doctor's bag, gloves, bandages, a lot of antibiotics, paracetamol, a blood pressure cuff, syringes.
para: Inside: a doctor's bag, gloves, bandages, a lot of antibiotics, paracetamol, a blood pressure cuff, syringes. And on the bottom shelf, a carton of IV fluid, clear bags, a litre each, the kind they had hung next to Granny when she had her gallbladder out.

options.label: Labels and dates
options.text: Inside: a doctor's bag, a box of gloves with the lid torn off, bandages, amoxicillin in four strengths, two of them past date, paracetamol by the hundred, a blood pressure cuff with the velcro gone furry, syringes still in their plastic.

options.label: Her reading, out loud
options.text: Inside: a doctor's bag, gloves, bandages, and she read the boxes as she went, out loud, the way she'd read the table. Amoxicillin. Co-amoxiclav. Metronidazole, expired March. Paracetamol, paracetamol, paracetamol. A blood pressure cuff. Syringes.

options.label: The one box that matters
options.text: Inside: a doctor's bag, gloves, bandages, antibiotics she knew the names of from the table and one she didn't, paracetamol, a blood pressure cuff, syringes, and a half-used box of something with Dr. Moss's own name on the label, which she put back without reading the rest.

why: Specific without stopping the scene. Option 2 is the most Juno but slows the walk to the bottom shelf, which is where the chapter is going.

note: one kid in this room should be doing something small and wrong — playing a game on a phone with the sound up, eating the Vales' food without asking, asking when the TV's going back on
anchor: The kitchen was full now, kids on every chair and along the walls, the Nettle girl asleep against Lonny with her thumb in her mouth.
para: The kitchen was full now, kids on every chair and along the walls, the Nettle girl asleep against Lonny with her thumb in her mouth. The baby had stopped screaming and was asleep on Tock's shoulder, and Tock hadn't moved in twenty minutes in case she woke.

options.label: Game sound up
options.text: One of the Pell boys had a game going on his phone with the sound up, little explosions, and nobody told him to stop.

options.label: Eating the Vales' food
options.text: Bix Hale was eating Granny's bread from the bag, standing at the counter, not asking, and he looked at Juno while he did it.

options.label: Asking about the TV
options.text: "When the TV coming back on?" one of the Nettles said, to nobody, for the third time, and for the third time nobody answered.

why: Bix has already been set up as the one who refuses, and Granny's bread is Granny's. Option 1 is the quietest; option 3 is already half-done by the chapter's 'nobody answered' beats.

note: one voice he used to hear every night up here is missing tonight — let him notice who, by name or boat
anchor: He had spent a lot of nights up here listening to people who didn't know they were being listened to.
para: The Quill house had a flat roof with a water tank and a satellite dish, and a plastic chair Fen had carried up there two years ago and never brought down. He brought the laptop and the dongle, a black thing the size of a lighter that his father had called a waste of money, and that Fen had bought with birthday money anyway, because with it and a length of wire you could hear anything in the air. Taxis. Aircraft. Fishing boats talking at four in the morning. He had spent a lot of nights up here listening to people who didn't know they were being listened to.

options.label: The boat that stays out
options.text: Most nights at ten a man on the *Dolores* called his wife on channel eight to say what he'd caught, and she told him to come in, and he stayed out. Tonight eight was hiss. Fen sat on it for a minute anyway.

options.label: The taxi driver he hated
options.text: There was a taxi driver, Pinto, who got on the base channel every night and talked about the price of parts and who was sleeping with who, and Fen had hated him for two years without ever seeing his face. He went looking for Pinto first. Nothing.

options.label: The Coast Guard check
options.text: The Coast Guard did a check on sixteen at ten every night, the same bored voice reading the same weather. Fen had timed his homework to it for a year. Ten came and went.

why: Pettiness is the edge the note asks for; the other two are absence, not meanness.

note: name the song — he'd know it by now and hate it
anchor: He went through the whole band, and it was the one song or nothing.
para: He started on FM, where the station was still playing the one song. He went through the whole band, and it was the one song or nothing.

options.label: Last Carnival's soca
options.text: He went through the whole band, and it was the same soca or nothing, the one from last Carnival about the woman with the red bucket, everywhere in February and hated by March. The station's overnight computer had been playing it since Sunday to nobody.

options.label: Nameless, but counted
options.text: He went through the whole band, and it was the one song or nothing. Twenty-three hours now. He knew the horn line better than his own phone number and would have paid money never to hear it again.

options.label: His mother's song
options.text: He went through the whole band, and it was the one song or nothing. The station's late filler, the Belafonte one, the one his mother used to sing at the sink. He had liked it once.

why: An invented song dates the island without going phonetic; the Belafonte one steals from the mother scene that follows.

note: what a dead pull does to the arm and shoulder — the cord's weight, the snap back
anchor: The second did nothing.
para: The garage was pitch black. He found the generator by memory, the yellow one on wheels his father ran on hurricane days and swore at, and he found the petrol can by its smell. He had watched his father do this a dozen times and never once done it himself. His hands shook on the cap. The first pull did nothing. The second did nothing. On the third the engine caught and roared, and he stood in the dark with his ears ringing and his eyes stinging from the fumes.

options.label: Knuckles on the housing
options.text: The second did nothing, and the cord came back hard enough to crack his knuckles against the housing.

options.label: Stops dead, shoulder
options.text: The second went halfway and stopped dead, the handle wrenched out of his fingers and snapped back into the housing, and the jolt went up into his shoulder.

options.label: Heavier than it looked
options.text: The second did nothing. The cord was heavier than it looked and it came back fast, and his arm already knew it would have to do this again.

why: One clause, one specific hurt; keeps the three-pull rhythm the paragraph is built on.

note: the made-up score — pay it off later, when someone wakes or when Kit tells her father anyway
anchor: Everton."
para: "Then I'll make one up," Sol said. "Two-one. Everton."

options.label: Seed it now, Kit's line
options.text: "He'd know," Kit said. "He'd know from your face."

options.label: Seed it now, Sol commits
options.text: "Two-one," Sol said again, so it would stick. "Late winner. He can have the goal if he wants it."

options.label: Pay it off later (beat-sheet note)
options.text: No change in ch 4. Beat sheet: the first time Kit sits with her father and talks to him (or if he wakes), she tells him two-one, Everton, late winner. Sol is in earshot and doesn't correct her.

why: The scene is already paying; the callback belongs where it costs something, three or four chapters on.

note: a naked stranger in a bath — give Sol or Lonny one line of awkwardness or pettiness about it before the pots
anchor: Lonny lifted him out, laid him on the bathroom floor and put a towel under his head, while Sol ran the tap to make sure the water still ran.
para: The Lark house was empty because the Lark kids were in the Mosses' front room with their baby. The next two were empty because the people in them had been at church in town on Sunday and had never come home, and Sol didn't want to think about where they were asleep. Her own were on the couch at number five, up the Trace, with the cricket still on. She had sat with them before she came to Juno's, an hour, her mother's hand in both of hers, and told her mother what she was going to do, because her mother liked a plan and liked it said out loud. Her mother ran the ice plant with a clipboard and a voice that made grown fishermen say yes ma'am, and had never once in sixteen years let Sol leave the house without knowing where she was going and when she'd be back. Strict, people said. Sol had never understood what they meant by it as a complaint. The fifth house had a man in the bath. Lonny lifted him out, laid him on the bathroom floor and put a towel under his head, while Sol ran the tap to make sure the water still ran. It did, and she filled every pot in the kitchen without discussing it, because that was what her mother would have done, and would have done an hour ago.

options.label: Lonny, not looking
options.text: "I'm not looking," Lonny said from the bathroom floor, looking. "When he wakes up, tell him I wasn't looking."

options.label: Sol, petty
options.text: He had a tan line like a vest and a woman's name on his arm that was not the name of the woman in the photo in the hall, and Sol decided, with the tap running, that she didn't like him.

options.label: Lonny, a whole man
options.text: "Towel," Lonny said. "Sol. Another towel. He's a whole man."

why: One line, in Lonny's register, and it lets the next sentence (the pots, her mother) land harder by contrast.

note: one obsessive specific of that room — the smell, the thermostat number, the sign on the door, what the floor does to rubber boots
anchor: She closed her eyes and thought about the cold room at the plant, the one at the back, where the ice came out in blocks and the air hurt your teeth and nobody talked because talking let the cold in.
para: The water was cool, like every tap on the island, and nothing more. She closed her eyes and thought about the cold room at the plant, the one at the back, where the ice came out in blocks and the air hurt your teeth and nobody talked because talking let the cold in. The room she went to when the world was too loud. She thought about the door shutting and the sound going away.

options.label: It smelled of nothing
options.text: It smelled of nothing. That was the thing about it. Every other room in the plant smelled of fish or diesel or somebody's lunch, and the cold room smelled of nothing at all.

options.label: Her mother's sign
options.text: Minus eighteen on the dial by the door, and under it her mother's sign in marker, DOOR SHUT MEANS DOOR SHUT, so old nobody read it any more.

options.label: Boots on the floor
options.text: The floor had a skin of ice on it that your boots squeaked on and then stuck to, so that you lifted your feet to walk and the whole room could hear you coming.

why: Smell is the sense nothing else in the scene uses, and 'nothing' is the right detail for the room she goes to for quiet.

note: what the thirst is in the mouth — tongue stuck to the roof, a taste, a sound when she swallows
anchor: She was thirstier than she had ever been in her life.
para: Her hands were burning, the way skin burns when it comes in from snow, which she had never seen, except on television. She was shaking. She was thirstier than she had ever been in her life. Lonny put a glass of water in her hand without a word. She drank it, he filled it, and she drank that too and the third one, her teeth chattering in a kitchen where the air was thirty degrees.

options.label: The click in the throat
options.text: She was thirstier than she had ever been in her life. When she swallowed, nothing went down, and she heard the click of it in her own throat.

options.label: Tongue stuck, metal taste
options.text: Her tongue was stuck to the roof of her mouth, and when she worked it loose the taste in there was metal and old pipe.

options.label: Lips on teeth
options.text: Her mouth had gone dry from the inside out, lips stuck to her teeth, and the first thing she did was lick them and the second was look for water.

why: Keeps the author's line and adds one sound; the sound is what the reader hasn't had yet.

note: after the third glass, one dry Lonny line would let the room breathe before Juno's question
anchor: She drank it, he filled it, and she drank that too and the third one, her teeth chattering in a kitchen where the air was thirty degrees.
para: Her hands were burning, the way skin burns when it comes in from snow, which she had never seen, except on television. She was shaking. She was thirstier than she had ever been in her life. Lonny put a glass of water in her hand without a word. She drank it, he filled it, and she drank that too and the third one, her teeth chattering in a kitchen where the air was thirty degrees.

options.label: That's nearly me
options.text: "Three," Lonny said, filling it again. "That's nearly me. Write that down, Juno."

options.label: The whole tank
options.text: "You going to drink the whole tank," Lonny said. "Then what we freezing."

options.label: Toilet tank
options.text: "If she does that to the toilet tank," Lonny said, to nobody, "I want to be told first."

why: Pays the formula gag from scene one, and Juno being told to write something down is the group's private register.

note: does it hit the eyes or the back of the throat first, and does it stop registering after five minutes inside — the thing a nurse knows
anchor: It was urine, mostly, sharp enough to make your eyes water when you came in from outside, and sweat, and under both of those something sweeter that Juno knew from the ward where Granny had her gallbladder out and had hoped never to smell again.
para: It got into everything. It was urine, mostly, sharp enough to make your eyes water when you came in from outside, and sweat, and under both of those something sweeter that Juno knew from the ward where Granny had her gallbladder out and had hoped never to smell again. Towels went under every sleeper. Towels came out wet. They were rinsed in buckets from the green rainwater pond on the quarry floor and hung along the quarry's chain-link fence, forty of them in a row. Nobody looked at the pond any more if they could help it. Tock had tied a T-shirt over his nose and mouth on the first morning, and nobody had laughed.

options.label: Eyes, then throat, then gone
options.text: It hit the eyes first, at the door, and the back of the throat a step later. Five minutes in you stopped smelling it, which was worse, because then you went out for a bucket and came back and it was waiting at the door like the first time. Urine, mostly, and sweat, and under both of those something sweeter that Juno knew from the ward where Granny had her gallbladder out and had hoped never to smell again.

options.label: The nose gives up
options.text: It went after five minutes. The nose gave up on it the way it had given up on the ward, and you forgot, until you came in from the quarry with a bucket and it was at the door again.

options.label: Read it off the kids' faces
options.text: Juno had stopped smelling it on the second day. She knew that because of what the little kids' faces did when they came in from outside.

why: Gives the nurse's knowledge (olfactory fatigue) as a thing that happens to her, and makes the smell an event each time, not a description.

note: this is the spot where Lonny dropping into heavier dialect would tell the reader something's wrong with him, per the bible rule
anchor: "Somebody with the name should do it."
para: "Same name as me," Lonny said. "We're not family. Never were. Everybody on the road used to make the joke." He shrugged, and it came out wrong, too big. "Somebody with the name should do it."

options.label: One word heavier
options.text: "Is somebody with the name should do it."

options.label: Heavier, said to the step
options.text: "Somebody with the name have to do it." He said it to the porch step, not to her.

options.label: Heavier and shuts the door
options.text: "Is somebody with the name should do it. Don't tell me no on that."

why: The smallest possible drop. One extra 'is' is enough for a reader who has heard Lonny for five chapters; the 'too big' shrug already does the rest.

note: what three hours of pickaxe does to palms under a dish towel — which hour the towel goes red, whether he swaps hands
anchor: He swung the pickaxe for three hours with his shirt off and his hands wrapped in a dish towel.
para: They chose the slope behind number nine, Mr. Hale's own house, under the lime tree at the bottom of his garden where the land fell away toward the sea. Lonny got a pickaxe and a spade from the Finches' garage. The first foot was easy, dark topsoil and roots. Under it the island was clay and stone, packed hard. He swung the pickaxe for three hours with his shirt off and his hands wrapped in a dish towel. The little kids brought him water in relays, then stood at the edge of the hole and watched, because nobody had told them not to.

options.label: Red by the second hour
options.text: The towel was red by the second hour. He swapped hands and it didn't help, because the other palm was open by then too, so he stopped swapping and swung.

options.label: Towel sticks, he doesn't look
options.text: After the first hour the towel stuck to him. He didn't take it off to look.

options.label: Seen later, under the tap
options.text: Nobody saw his hands until after, under the tap, when the water ran off them pink for a while and then clear.

why: Pays off the tap-under-the-tank beat that is already in the chapter, and keeps the kids-watching line as the paragraph's end.

note: the red ball — if it isn't seeded in ch 1–4, one line there would make this land harder
anchor: He kept it for a year."
para: "He kept the good one," Juno said. "The red one. Remember? Form One. He kept it for a year."

options.label: Lonny cried about it
options.text:
"You cried," Tock said.

"I didn't cry."

options.label: He gave it back at Christmas
options.text: "Gave it back at Christmas," Tock said. "Said he found it."

why: Makes the ball land inside this scene without a seed: the old man kept it a year and then pretended to find it, which is the whole man in one line and goes straight into the laugh. The seed in ch 1–4 is a separate, earlier edit.

note: petrol after-taste — where it actually sits hours later, burps, the back of the throat
anchor: He could still taste it, more in his nose than his mouth.
para: That afternoon he and Lonny had siphoned Mr. Finch's Pajero, which was old and gave up forty litres without a fight, and Dr. Moss's Corolla, which was new and had a valve in the neck of the tank that stopped the hose. Fen had sucked on the hose anyway, because he hadn't known about the valve, and got a mouthful of petrol that had nothing to do with the car. He had spat in the Mosses' drain for ten minutes. He could still taste it, more in his nose than his mouth.

options.label: Behind the nose, in burps
options.text: He could still taste it. It sat behind his nose now, and every burp brought it up new.

options.label: Back of the throat, bread won't move it
options.text: Six hours later it was still there, at the back of his throat, and bread hadn't moved it.

options.label: Stopped being surprised
options.text: He could still taste it. His burps tasted of it. He had stopped being surprised by that around eight.

why: Petrol lives in the sinuses and comes back with every burp for a day; the shortest version says both.

note: what the AIS screen actually looks like on a dongle — the software, the triangles, the stale timestamps
anchor: He pulled up the map.
para: He put the binoculars down and opened the laptop. The dongle could pick up AIS, the signal every big ship sent out with its name and speed and where it was going. He had spent whole nights watching cargo ships crawl across the screen toward Panama. He pulled up the map.

options.label: The software and the triangles
options.text: He pulled up the map. OpenCPN, the free one, grey sea and a yellow coastline, every ship a small green triangle with its name beside it and a line out of its nose for where it was going.

options.label: Stale timestamps
options.text: He pulled up the map. The triangles were still on it from the last time he'd looked, each one with a time beside it in grey, five days old, the last time anybody had heard from it.

options.label: One dead ship still pointing at Panama
options.text: The last triangle on the screen was a bulk carrier called *Ocean Pride*, eleven days stale, still pointing at Panama.

why: The stale timestamps do double work: they show the screen and they show the world has stopped, before the empty horizon lands.

note: Fen's one dry line for the chapter could land here, before Lyra runs
anchor: he said.
para: "It's the navy," he said.

options.label: Not ours
options.text: "It's a navy," he said. "Not ours. We don't have one."

options.label: Wave at them
options.text: "It's the navy," he said. "Wave. They might wave back."

options.label: It's grey
options.text: "It's grey," he said. "That's all I know. It's grey."

why: Dry, true, and Lyra can run off happy on 'navy' without hearing the rest, which is the scene.

note: one small meanness in the painting — a kid who won't share the brush, or someone who says the sheet is a waste of paint
anchor: Nobody asked him what he thought it would do, and he didn't say.
para: The kids took turns watching it from the Hales' balcony, two at a time, with the binoculars Fen let them borrow. In the afternoon Ida Moss and the Nettle girl and half the little ones painted a bedsheet with house paint from the Finches' garage and laid it out on the flat white floor of the quarry, weighed down with bricks: *24 KIDS. SEND HELP*. Twenty-four was Juno's number. It was in the book under Day 7, with thirteen and twenty and twenty-two crossed out above it. Fen carried the paint tins and held one corner of the sheet while the Nettle girl did the S. Nobody asked him what he thought it would do, and he didn't say.

options.label: Kicked tin, grey K
options.text: Bix wanted the S and the Nettle girl wouldn't give up the brush, so he kicked the tin, and a leg of the K went grey, and they left it.

options.label: Olli says it's a waste
options.text: Olli said it was a waste of paint. Nobody answered, so he said it again, louder, and Ida told him to go and sit down.

options.label: Painted over without a word
options.text: The Nettle boy did the 2 and did it backwards, and his sister painted over it without saying anything to him, which was worse than saying something.

why: The grey leg of the K is a flaw the drone will photograph; it is the kind of small wrong thing a sheet made by kids would actually have.

note: the cylinder itself — colour, the chipped paint, the brand stamp — the thing a boy who's watched Granny change it a hundred times would know by heart
anchor: He went two doors down, came back with it on his shoulder and got down on the kitchen floor to change it.
para: The cylinder under the counter was empty. He knew it before he tipped it; it was too light, it rocked like a drum. There were thirteen more cylinders in the other eight kitchens on the road. Juno had a list of them in the exercise book, one a day, and the next one on the list was the Pells'. He went two doors down, came back with it on his shoulder and got down on the kitchen floor to change it.

options.label: The Pells' cylinder, specifically
options.text: He went two doors down and came back with the Pells' cylinder on his shoulder, a blue one, the paint gone to rust at the foot ring where it had stood in water, and got down on the kitchen floor to change it.

options.label: Granny's versus theirs
options.text: He went two doors down, came back with it on his shoulder and got down on the kitchen floor to change it. It was the wrong colour. Granny's had always been the red one with the dent in the collar, and this one was blue and smelled of somebody else's kitchen.

options.label: Weight and the walk
options.text: He went two doors down, got the Pells' cylinder up onto his shoulder the way Granny said never to, and came back with twenty kilos of steel grinding on his collarbone. He got down on the kitchen floor to change it.

why: One concrete cylinder the reader can see, and the rust foot ring is the kind of thing only a boy who has watched it for years would know.

note: what skin does when it should hurt and doesn't — tight? thick, like after a long time in cold water? only you know this one
anchor: They didn't hurt at all.
para: He looked at his hands. They were red across the palms, like he'd been clapping too hard. They didn't hurt. They didn't hurt at all.

options.label: Thick, far away
options.text: They felt thick, the way your hand feels when you've slept on it, there but a long way off.

options.label: Skin too tight
options.text: The skin was tight across the palms, pulled, like the skin on hot milk. When he closed his fingers it didn't crack.

options.label: He checks, and nothing
options.text: They didn't hurt at all. He pressed a thumb into the middle of his left palm, hard, and the white mark came and went and that was all.

why: An action instead of an adjective: he tests it, and the test says the same thing the sentence does.

note: name the smell once, one noun — whatever a room of fourteen unwashed sleepers and a teaspoon-fed ward actually smells of by day six
anchor: The ward was empty except for the sleepers and the smell.
para: The ward was empty except for the sleepers and the smell. Everyone who could walk was up on the road looking at the sea. The windows were open and the curtains moved. Fourteen people on mattresses, breathing slow. Mr. Hale's place by the wall had a clean sheet on it now, folded, and nobody had moved anyone into it.

options.label: Urine and Dettol
options.text: The ward was empty except for the sleepers and the smell, which was urine under Dettol, and under that something sweet that was the sleepers themselves.

options.label: Sour milk
options.text: The ward was empty except for the sleepers and the smell. Sour milk. Fourteen mouths fed off a teaspoon for six days, and no one brushing their teeth.

options.label: Smell as a thing he walks into
options.text: The ward was empty except for the sleepers, and the smell met him at the door, warm, the smell of a bedroom nobody had opened, under the Dettol Juno kept wiping over it.

why: Sour milk is the teaspoon ward in one noun, and it is the smell Tock, who boils the bottles, would name first.

note: this is the crib-cost rule from the bible — make sure the reader has already seen that crib in ch 1 or 2 so this lands as memory, not news
anchor: He thought about the crib in the Pells' house on the first night, which he had walked past.
para: They found out in Granny's kitchen, with the door shut and the cylinder turned off. He put both hands on the sides of the big pot while Ida stood by the sink with her arms folded, and he tried to be angry. He thought about the regulator. He thought about the crib in the Pells' house on the first night, which he had walked past. His hands went hot, too hot. The water went from still to boiling in two seconds and spat and burned his wrists. He let go and swore, and Ida said "Language," without looking up.

options.label: Keep, sharpen the memory
options.text: He thought about the crib in the Pells' back room on the first night, the one he had looked straight at from the doorway with a torch and walked past.

options.label: Make it a thing he carries
options.text: He thought about the crib in the Pells' house on the first night. He had walked past it. He had gone back for the cylinder today and walked past it again, and it was still there, and nobody said the word Pell on this road any more.

why: Reads as memory either way; the torch and the doorway give the reader a picture to match against ch 1 or 2. Separate check needed: the crib must already be on the page in ch 1 or 2, which is outside this chapter.

note: one Lonny line here, before Fen comes in, so the quiet after the news has something to fall from
anchor: Tock at the end, with his hands flat on Granny's table and Vee asleep on a pile of towels in the living room, right next door, where he could hear her breathing through the open door.
para: All of them except Lyra, who was home with their mother. Juno at the head, where Granny used to sit, with the exercise book. Lonny with his chair tipped back against the wall. Sol with her knees up on her chair. Tock at the end, with his hands flat on Granny's table and Vee asleep on a pile of towels in the living room, right next door, where he could hear her breathing through the open door.

options.label: Lonny on the oven gloves
options.text:
"You could just wear the gloves," Lonny said. "The chilli ones. Nobody would say anything."

"Sol would say something."

"I'd say something," Sol said.

options.label: Lonny on the table
options.text: "Don't touch the table," Lonny said. "That's mahogany. Granny will wake up for that one."

options.label: Lonny on Vee's breathing
options.text:
"She snores," Lonny said, tipping his head at the door. "Like Mr. Hale. You hear it?"

"She doesn't snore."

"She snores, Tock. It's in the family."

why: One line, and it sets up the handprints on the mahogany ten lines later without anybody pointing at it.

note: Tock carries the most dialect on the hill, and the rule says a Trace kid dropping heavier means something is wrong with them — this is the spot; if he says anything out loud here, let it come out in the heaviest voice he has in the book
anchor: It came from the word *nice* in the mouth of somebody he had never met who had two hundred kids and a radio and a harbour full of fellas who did what he said, and who wanted his sister, and who thought he could send somebody up this hill and get her.
para: The heat came up in Tock so fast he didn't feel it start. It came from his stomach, from the place where it lived. It came from the word *nice* in the mouth of somebody he had never met who had two hundred kids and a radio and a harbour full of fellas who did what he said, and who wanted his sister, and who thought he could send somebody up this hill and get her.

options.label: One line, heaviest voice
options.text: "Let him send," Tock said. "Let him send who he want. Dey could come up de hill and ask me nice."

options.label: He repeats the word
options.text: "Nice," Tock said. "He go ask she nice." Nobody at the table had heard him talk like that since Granny went down.

options.label: Quiet, to Fen
options.text: "Two nights," Tock said, and it came out the way Granny's people talked, from the back of the throat. "Two nights yuh sit on dat, Fen."

why: Keeps the rage pointed at Judge, not Fen, and the dialect drop does the work the bible asks for without the narrator saying so.

note: what electrical tape does on a sweaty, hairy forearm — does it even hold?
anchor: She splinted it as the picture showed and taped it before she could start wishing she had done it a week ago.
para: Lonny leaned his whole weight into the boy's shoulders. Juno set her knee against the concrete and pulled the way you pull a car door that has jammed in the heat, steady and then all at once, and something gave under her hands with a soft wet crack she felt in her teeth before she heard it. The arm was straight. It was straighter. It was as straight as she was going to get it, and she knew that while it was happening. She splinted it as the picture showed and taped it before she could start wishing she had done it a week ago.

options.label: Tape won't hold on sweat
options.text: She splinted it as the picture showed. The tape wouldn't take on the boy's arm, the sweat lifted it as fast as she laid it, so she wound it round and round over itself until the slats stopped moving, before she could start wishing she had done it a week ago.

options.label: Tape over the hair
options.text: She splinted it as the picture showed and taped it, and the tape went down over the hair on his arm and he would scream again when it came off, and she taped it anyway, before she could start wishing she had done it a week ago.

options.label: Judge's thumb
options.text: She splinted it as the picture showed. Judge held the end of the tape down with his thumb while she wound it, because it would not stick to wet skin, and neither of them said anything about that. She taped it before she could start wishing she had done it a week ago.

why: True to the material, and it costs Juno something small and physical in the moment.

note: one kid in the ring says something petty here — "that's it?" — before the crowd breaks up
anchor: The boy was crying and saying thank you, thank you, and she didn't know what to do with that, so she said, "Don't climb walls."
para: She sat back on her heels with her hands shaking. The boy was crying and saying thank you, thank you, and she didn't know what to do with that, so she said, "Don't climb walls."

options.label: That's it?
options.text:
"That's it?" somebody said from the back of the ring, a boy, bored already. "She just pull it?"

Nobody answered him. The ring broke up.

options.label: It still crooked
options.text: "It still crooked," a girl said, from somewhere behind Lonny. She wasn't wrong. Judge didn't look round, and the ring broke up.

options.label: Judge shuts it down
options.text:
"That's it?" somebody said from the back.

"Go and catch fish," Judge said, without turning, and the ring broke up.

why: The petty line is also true, and Juno already knows it; the girl saying it out loud in front of fifty kids is the small cruelty the scene wants.

note: Ria's name on the wrist wants paying off within three chapters — the ink fading, or the night Nell sends
anchor: She held the girl's hand until the girl closed her eyes, and wrote the name on the inside of her own wrist in Nell's pencil so she would have to look at it later.
para: She didn't answer, because the true answer was *nothing*, and Ria was looking at her. She held the girl's hand until the girl closed her eyes, and wrote the name on the inside of her own wrist in Nell's pencil so she would have to look at it later.

options.label: Plant it in the last scene
options.text: [Add to the final paragraph of the chapter, after "with the notebook on her chest":] The pencil on her wrist had smudged to a grey mark on the walk home. She could still read it.

options.label: Plant it at the bend
options.text: [Add to the bend paragraph, after "and kept walking":] She turned her wrist over as she passed, and the name was still there, greyer.

why: A second touch in the same chapter makes it a thread rather than a gesture; the real payoff (Nell sends, or the mark is gone and so is Ria) still belongs to ch 9–11 and needs a beat-sheet entry.
